claim: TRPV1 is a polymodal nociceptor for a wide range of physical and chemical stimuli.
source: TRPV1 is a polymodal nociceptor for a wide range of physical and chemical stimuli (Caterina et al., 1997; Tominaga et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caterina et al., 1997 and Tominaga et al., 1998

claim: TRPV1's unique sensitivity to capsaicin underlies spicy and hot sensation.
source: Its unique sensitivity to the pungent chili compound capsaicin underlies spicy and hot sensation, and has been used for topical pain treatment through desensitization (Derry et al., 2017; Mason et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Derry et al., 2017 and Mason et al., 2004

claim: Capsaicin has been used for topical pain treatment through desensitization.
source: Its unique sensitivity to the pungent chili compound capsaicin underlies spicy and hot sensation, and has been used for topical pain treatment through desensitization (Derry et al., 2017; Mason et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Derry et al., 2017 and Mason et al., 2004

claim: Capsaicin induces TRPV1 activation with near unity open probability at saturating concentrations.
source: Capsaicin-induced TRPV1 activation represents an outstanding case of ligand-receptor interaction in terms of efficacy (near unity open probability at saturating concentrations), potency (EC50 at about 100 nM), and ligand discrimination (closely related compounds acting as either an agonist or an antagonist) (Yang and Zheng, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang and Zheng, 2017

claim: Capsaicin activates TRPV1 with an EC50 of about 100 nM.
source: Capsaicin-induced TRPV1 activation represents an outstanding case of ligand-receptor interaction in terms of efficacy (near unity open probability at saturating concentrations), potency (EC50 at about 100 nM), and ligand discrimination (closely related compounds acting as either an agonist or an antagonist) (Yang and Zheng, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang and Zheng, 2017

claim: TRPV1's ligand-binding pocket resides within the transmembrane domain.
source: Unlike most well-studied ligand-gated ion channels with extracellular or intracellular ligand-binding domains (Chen and Gouaux, 1997; Meyerson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Zagotta et al., 2003), TRPV1's ligand-binding pocket resides within the transmembrane domain, formed by the S3 and S4 segments and the S4-S5 linker from the same subunit, as well as the S5 and S6 segments from a neighboring subunit due to a domain-swapping subunit arrangement (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: TRPV1's ligand-binding pocket is formed by the S3 and S4 segments and the S4-S5 linker from the same subunit, as well as the S5 and S6 segments from a neighboring subunit.
source: Unlike most well-studied ligand-gated ion channels with extracellular or intracellular ligand-binding domains (Chen and Gouaux, 1997; Meyerson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Zagotta et al., 2003), TRPV1's ligand-binding pocket resides within the transmembrane domain, formed by the S3 and S4 segments and the S4-S5 linker from the same subunit, as well as the S5 and S6 segments from a neighboring subunit due to a domain-swapping subunit arrangement (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: TRPV1 has a domain-swapping subunit arrangement.
source: Unlike most well-studied ligand-gated ion channels with extracellular or intracellular ligand-binding domains (Chen and Gouaux, 1997; Meyerson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Zagotta et al., 2003), TRPV1's ligand-binding pocket resides within the transmembrane domain, formed by the S3 and S4 segments and the S4-S5 linker from the same subunit, as well as the S5 and S6 segments from a neighboring subunit due to a domain-swapping subunit arrangement (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: TRPV1 functions as an allosteric protein where capsaicin binding induces a conformational change in the ligand-binding pocket that promotes opening of the activation gate.
source: TRPV1 functions as an allosteric protein: binding of capsaicin induces a conformational change in the ligand-binding pocket that allosterically promotes the opening of the adjacent activation gate (Latorre et al., 2007; Matta and Ahern, 2007; Cao et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010; Jara-Oseguera and Islas, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Latorre et al., 2007; Matta and Ahern, 2007; Cao et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010; Jara-Oseguera and Islas, 2013

claim: Capsaicin and related pungent plant compounds can activate TRPV1 in two different ligand poses inside the ligand-binding pocket.
source: Activation of TRPV1 can be induced by capsaicin and related pungent plant compounds in two different ligand poses inside the ligand-binding pocket (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and previous studies cited in the text

claim: In the 'head-down tail-up' vertical pose, capsaicin bridges the S4 segment and the S4-S5 linker with two hydrogen bonds.
source: In this 'head-down tail-up' vertical pose, the bound ligand bridges the S4 segment and the S4-S5 linker with two hydrogen bonds, one between the amide group in the capsaicin neck and the hydroxyl group of T551 on the TRPV1 S4 segment (using mTRPV1 amino acid number) and another between the hydroxyl group in the capsaicin head and the carboxyl group of E571 on the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and citations in the text

claim: One hydrogen bond forms between the amide group in the capsaicin neck and the hydroxyl group of T551 on the TRPV1 S4 segment.
source: In this 'head-down tail-up' vertical pose, the bound ligand bridges the S4 segment and the S4-S5 linker with two hydrogen bonds, one between the amide group in the capsaicin neck and the hydroxyl group of T551 on the TRPV1 S4 segment (using mTRPV1 amino acid number) and another between the hydroxyl group in the capsaicin head and the carboxyl group of E571 on the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and citations in the text

claim: Another hydrogen bond forms between the hydroxyl group in the capsaicin head and the carboxyl group of E571 on the S4-S5 linker.
source: In this 'head-down tail-up' vertical pose, the bound ligand bridges the S4 segment and the S4-S5 linker with two hydrogen bonds, one between the amide group in the capsaicin neck and the hydroxyl group of T551 on the TRPV1 S4 segment (using mTRPV1 amino acid number) and another between the hydroxyl group in the capsaicin head and the carboxyl group of E571 on the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and citations in the text

claim: Simultaneous formation of two hydrogen bonds lifts the S4-S5 linker upward and outward.
source: Simultaneous formation of these two hydrogen bonds lifts the S4-S5 linker upward and outward, a process analogous to voltage activation of Kv channels (Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2003

claim: The S4-S5 linker movement reduces the distance between T551 and E571 by 1.3 Å.
source: The S4-S5 linker movement reduces the distance between the hydrogen bond-forming sidechains of T551 and E571 by 1.3 Å, as shown by comparing the cryo-EM structures of TRPV1 in the apo and capsaicin-bound states (Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1B

claim: Movement of the S4-S5 linker away from the pore leads to subsequent S6 movement and pore opening.
source: Movement of the S4-S5 linker away from the pore leads to subsequent S6 movement and pore opening (Yang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018

claim: Piperine from black peppers uses a less efficacious horizontal ligand pose involving direct interaction with the S6 segment.
source: A less efficacious ligand pose, used by piperine from black peppers (and zingerone from gingers), involves direct interaction with the S6 segment instead of the S4-S5 linker (Yin et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yin et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2019

claim: In the horizontal pose, piperine bridges T551 on the S4 segment and T671 in the middle of the S6 segment.
source: In this horizontal pose, piperine is found to bridge T551 on the S4 segment and T671 in the middle of the S6 segment, which is expected to cause S6 movement and pore opening.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on piperine

claim: E571A mutation strongly affected activation by capsaicin but not piperine.
source: In support of the existence of these two distinct ligand poses, preventing hydrogen bond formation with the S4-S5 linker by an E571A mutation strongly affected activation by capsaicin but not piperine, whereas mutations at T671 (to S or V) on S6 disrupted activation by piperine but had little effects on activation by capsaicin (Yang et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2019

claim: Mutations at T671 (to S or V) on S6 disrupted activation by piperine but had little effects on activation by capsaicin.
source: In support of the existence of these two distinct ligand poses, preventing hydrogen bond formation with the S4-S5 linker by an E571A mutation strongly affected activation by capsaicin but not piperine, whereas mutations at T671 (to S or V) on S6 disrupted activation by piperine but had little effects on activation by capsaicin (Yang et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2019

claim: Cap+1 contains one extra -CH2 group between the hydrogen-bond-forming groups compared to capsaicin.
source: In order to understand why different agonists take distinct binding poses, and how these poses allow ligands to stabilize the open conformation of the ligand-binding pocket, we designed two capsaicin analogs with an altered neck length (Figure 1C): Cap+1 contains one extra -CH2 group between the hydrogen-bond-forming groups, whereas Cap-1 contains one less -CH2 group between the hydrogen-bond-forming groups.
evidence: Supported by description of molecular design and Figure 1C

claim: Cap-1 contains one less -CH2 group between the hydrogen-bond-forming groups compared to capsaicin.
source: In order to understand why different agonists take distinct binding poses, and how these poses allow ligands to stabilize the open conformation of the ligand-binding pocket, we designed two capsaicin analogs with an altered neck length (Figure 1C): Cap+1 contains one extra -CH2 group between the hydrogen-bond-forming groups, whereas Cap-1 contains one less -CH2 group between the hydrogen-bond-forming groups.
evidence: Supported by description of molecular design and Figure 1C

claim: Changes in the neck length of Cap+1 and Cap-1 (±1 C-C bond length) are compatible to the 1.3 Å movement of the S4-S5 linker from the closed state to the open state.
source: Changes in the neck length of these compounds (±1 C-C bond length) are compatible to the 1.3 Å movement of the S4-S5 linker from the closed state to the open state.
evidence: Supported by comparison of structural changes

claim: The structural changes in Cap+1 and Cap-1 preserved all the key functional groups involved in direct ligand-channel interactions.
source: Importantly, these structural changes preserved all the key functional groups involved in direct ligand-channel interactions.
evidence: Supported by description of molecular design

claim: Both Cap+1 and Cap-1 strongly activated TRPV1.
source: Both Cap+1 and Cap-1 strongly activated TRPV1 by binding to the same binding site as capsaicin (confirmed by competition with capsazepine; see Figure 4B below).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 4B

claim: Cap+1 and Cap-1 bind to the same binding site as capsaicin.
source: Both Cap+1 and Cap-1 strongly activated TRPV1 by binding to the same binding site as capsaicin (confirmed by competition with capsazepine; see Figure 4B below).
evidence: Supported by competition experiments with capsazepine and reference to Figure 4B

claim: Capsaicin activated mouse TRPV1 with an EC50 value of 0.14 ± 0.01 µM.
source: As previously reported (Yang et al., 2015), capsaicin activated mouse TRPV1 with an EC50 value of 0.14 ± 0.01 µM and an open probability (Po) of 0.94 (Figure 2B and F), comparable to observations from the rat TRPV1 (Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Geron et al., 2018; Morales-Lázaro et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by experimental data, citations to Yang et al., 2015 and references to Figure 2B and F

claim: Capsaicin activated mouse TRPV1 with an open probability (Po) of 0.94.
source: As previously reported (Yang et al., 2015), capsaicin activated mouse TRPV1 with an EC50 value of 0.14 ± 0.01 µM and an open probability (Po) of 0.94 (Figure 2B and F), comparable to observations from the rat TRPV1 (Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Geron et al., 2018; Morales-Lázaro et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by experimental data, citations to Yang et al., 2015 and references to Figure 2B and F

claim: Cap-1 activated the channel at a similar concentration range compared to capsaicin.
source: Cap-1 activated the channel at a similar concentration range compared to capsaicin; however, the maximal currents induced by Cap-1 were smaller by about 10% (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2A

claim: The maximal currents induced by Cap-1 were smaller by about 10% compared to capsaicin.
source: Cap-1 activated the channel at a similar concentration range compared to capsaicin; however, the maximal currents induced by Cap-1 were smaller by about 10% (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2A

claim: The reduced maximal current amplitude for Cap-1 was likely caused by a slightly lower single-channel conductance.
source: We found that the reduced maximal current amplitude was likely caused by a slightly lower single-channel conductance (Figure 2C,D,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 2C, D, F

claim: After correction for the conductance difference, macroscopic responses to CAP-1 exhibited similar maximal Po and EC50 values to capsaicin responses.
source: After correction for the conductance difference, macroscopic responses to CAP-1 exhibited similar maximal Po and EC50 values to capsaicin responses (Figure 2B and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 2B and F

claim: Cap+1 activated TRPV1 to similar single-channel conductance and maximal Po as capsaicin.
source: Cap+1 activated TRPV1 to similar single-channel conductance and maximal Po as capsaicin (Figure 2A and C); however, it took much higher concentrations of Cap+1 to reach the maximal Po level (Figure 2B and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 2A, C, B, and F

claim: It took much higher concentrations of Cap+1 to reach the maximal Po level compared to capsaicin.
source: Cap+1 activated TRPV1 to similar single-channel conductance and maximal Po as capsaicin (Figure 2A and C); however, it took much higher concentrations of Cap+1 to reach the maximal Po level (Figure 2B and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 2A, C, B, and F

claim: Lengthening the capsaicin neck by one C-C bond length (Cap+1) reduced potency but did not affect the maximal Po.
source: Therefore, lengthening and shortening the capsaicin neck by one C-C bond length did not disrupt ligand-channel interactions but appeared to have altered the nature of the interactions. Furthermore, it is interesting to observe that lengthening the ligand (CAP+1) did not affect the maximal Po (as one might expect if the extended ligand is a better fit to the closed-state ligand-binding pocket), but instead reduced potency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Rosetta modeling predicted a capsaicin-like vertical binding pose for Cap-1 with hydrogen bonds to T551 and E571.
source: Among the top models, we found similar binding poses as that of capsaicin, with Cap-1 or Cap+1 in a 'head-down tail-up' vertical pose (Figure 3A and D, upper panels; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1, left panel). In this orientation, the agonist formed hydrogen bonds with T551 and E571 to stabilize the upward conformation of the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and references to Figure 3A and D

claim: T551V or E571A mutations dramatically increased EC50 and decreased Po_max for Cap-1 and Cap+1.
source: This capsaicin-like binding pose could be functionally confirmed. When T551 or E571 was mutated to a nonpolar residue to prevent hydrogen bond formation at these two positions, the concentration-response curves for Cap-1 or Cap+1 were dramatically affected: we observed a one to two orders of magnitude increase in EC50 and a large decrease in Po_max (Figure 3C and F; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 3C, F and Table 1

claim: Rosetta modeling predicted a semi-horizontal pose for Cap-1 in which it forms a hydrogen bond with T671 on S6.
source: For Cap-1, Rosetta modeling predicted a semi-horizontal pose in which it forms a hydrogen bond with T671 on S6 using the carbonyl oxygen atom in its neck (Figure 3A, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and reference to Figure 3A

claim: In the semi-horizontal pose, the Cap-1 head is located in the vicinity of the S2-S3 linker where it interacts with Y512.
source: The Cap-1 head is located in the vicinity of the S2-S3 linker where it interacts with Y512.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: T671S and Y512F mutations right-shifted the concentration-response curve for Cap-1 by two orders of magnitude.
source: Functional data were supportive of the presence of this binding pose: conserved mutations T671S and Y512F right-shifted the concentration-response curve by two orders of magnitude (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 3C and supplementary figures

claim: T671S had no effect on capsaicin activation.
source: In comparison, T671S had no effect on capsaicin activation, whereas Y512F had a minor effect (Yang et al., 2015; Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015 and references to supplementary figures

claim: Y512F had a minor effect on capsaicin activation.
source: In comparison, T671S had no effect on capsaicin activation, whereas Y512F had a minor effect (Yang et al., 2015; Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015 and references to supplementary figures

claim: Cap+1 was predicted to interact with T671 on S6 with a hydrogen bond formed with the oxygen atom in the head hydroxyl group.
source: Cap+1 was predicted to also interact with T671 on S6 with a hydrogen bond, which is formed with the oxygen atom in the head hydroxyl group (Figure 3D, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and reference to Figure 3D

claim: Binding energy distribution indicates that Cap+1 interacts predominantly with T671 instead of E571 on the S4-S5 linker.
source: Indeed, binding energy distribution indicates that Cap+1 interacts predominantly with T671 instead of E571 on the S4-S5 linker (Figure 3E; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1, right panel).

claim: In the horizontal pose, the Cap+1 neck forms a hydrogen bond with T551 and establishes VDW interactions with Y555.
source: In this horizontal pose, the Cap+1 neck forms a hydrogen bond with T551 and establishes VDW interactions with the nearby Y555.

claim: T671S and T551V mutations right-shifted the concentration-response curve for Cap+1 by two orders of magnitude and reduced the maximal Po.

evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 3F and supplementary figure

claim: The tail of Cap+1 is predicted to be unable to fully extend into the hydrophobic region in the upper ligand-binding pocket in the horizontal pose.
source: We noticed that in this pose the tail of Cap+1 is predicted to be unable to fully extend into the hydrophobic region in the upper ligand-binding pocket.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: The capsaicin tail contributes substantially to binding via VDW interactions with the heavily hydrophobic upper part of ligand-binding pocket.
source: For capsaicin, we have previously found that its tail contributes substantially to binding via VDW interactions with the heavily hydrophobic upper part of ligand-binding pocket (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015

claim: Reducing VDW interactions might be part of the reason that Cap+1 binds much less tightly than capsaicin and Cap-1.
source: Reducing these VDW interactions might be part of the reason that Cap+1 binds much less tightly than capsaicin and Cap-1.
evidence: Supported by inference from computational modeling and experimental data

claim: The OFF rates for Cap-1 and Cap+1 were two to six times faster than that of capsaicin.
source: We found that the OFF rates for Cap-1 and Cap+1 were two to six times faster than that of capsaicin (Figure 4A), indicating that binding of these analogs is less stable.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 4A

claim: Capsazepine could compete off both Cap-1 and Cap+1 more easily than capsaicin.
source: We found that capsazepine could compete off both Cap-1 and Cap+1 more easily than capsaicin (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 4B

claim: Both Cap-1 and Cap+1 bind less tightly to TRPV1 compared to capsaicin.
source: With I574A-containing channels, we found that both Cap-1 and Cap+1 produced a concentration-response curve that was right-shifted, consistent with a higher KD and weaker binding, a conclusion consistent with unbinding analyses described above (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 4D and E

claim: Cap+1 exhibited a lower efficacy compared to that of capsaicin, reflecting that L was much reduced for Cap+1.
source: In addition, Cap+1 exhibited a lower efficacy compared to that of capsaicin, reflecting that L was much reduced for Cap+1 (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to Figure 4D and F

claim: Cap+1 is less powerful in inducing the activation allosteric transition upon binding compared to capsaicin.
source: In summary, both Cap-1 and Cap+1 bind less tightly to TRPV1, and Cap+1 is also less powerful in inducing the activation allosteric transition upon binding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: While both CAP-1 and CAP+1 adopted drastically different poses, the binding pocket itself appeared to be in very similar conformations among the top models.

claim: The maximal deviation from the capsaicin-bound conformation was within 1 Å for Cap-1 and Cap+1 bound structures.
source: The maximal deviation from the capsaicin-bound conformation was within 1 Å.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Residues with a higher degree of deviation were all clustered around T551, E571, and T671, indicating the occurrence of local side-chain adaptations to accommodate each ligand molecule.
source: Interestingly, it is noticed that residues with a higher degree of deviation were all clustered around T551, E571, and T671, the three sites of ligand interactions, indicating the occurrence of local side-chain adaptations to accommodate each ligand molecule.

source: The observation that structurally distinct ligands stabilize a single permissive conformation in the TRPV1 ligand-binding pocket suggests that there is a dominant low-energy conformation when a vanilloid molecule replaces the endogenous lipid molecule.

source: The observation that structurally distinct ligands stabilize a single permissive conformation in the TRPV1 ligand-binding pocket suggests that there is a dominant low-energy conformation when a vanilloid molecule replaces the endogenous lipid molecule.

claim: Cap-1 and Cap+1 induced currents revealed similar cation selectivity and permeability as capsaicin induced currents.
source: Functional analyses of Cap-1 and Cap+1 induced currents revealed similar cation selectivity and permeability as capsaicin induced currents (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: A number of endovanilloids such as anandamide and 12-HEPTE have been reported to target TRPV1 to produce some of their physiological functions.
source: In particular, a number of endovanilloids such as anandamide and 12-HEPTE have been reported to target TRPV1 to produce some of their physiological functions that could be antagonized by capsazepine or iodo-resiniferatoxin (Lam et al., 2007; Hwang et al., 2000; Jennings et al., 2003).

claim: The stability of an open pore is linked to the stability of the permissive conformation of the ligand-binding pocket.

claim: The stability of the permissive conformation of the ligand-binding pocket is determined by molecular interactions between ligand and its surrounding channel residues.

claim: In glutamate receptors, structurally distinct ligands bind in similar poses and induce graded conformational changes in the ligand-binding domain to produce graded channel activities.
source: Outstanding examples include glutamate receptors, for which structurally distinct ligands bind in similar poses and induce graded conformational changes in the ligand-binding domain to produce graded channel activities, and these multiple ligand-binding domain conformations define partial and full agonists (Jin et al., 2003; Armstrong and Gouaux, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin et al., 2003; Armstrong and Gouaux, 2000

claim: Multiple ligand-binding domain conformations define partial and full agonists in glutamate receptors.
source: Outstanding examples include glutamate receptors, for which structurally distinct ligands bind in similar poses and induce graded conformational changes in the ligand-binding domain to produce graded channel activities, and these multiple ligand-binding domain conformations define partial and full agonists (Jin et al., 2003; Armstrong and Gouaux, 2000).

claim: There exists a single stable permissive conformation for the TRPV1 ligand-binding pocket.
source: Nonetheless, these distinct ligand-binding poses all support a single permissive ligand-binding pocket conformation. These observations argue for a single stable permissive conformation for the TRPV1 ligand-binding pocket, one that the cryo-EM structures of capsaicin- and RTX-bound channels demonstrated (Gao et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2013).

claim: Ligands that better stabilize the ligand-binding pocket in its permissive conformation are expected to yield a more stable pore conformation and induce stronger channel activation.
source: Ligands that better stabilize the ligand-binding pocket in its permissive conformation are expected to yield a more stable pore conformation and induce stronger channel activation.

claim: Conformational changes in the TRPV1 pore are thought to involve movements of S6 and the selectivity filter.
source: Conformational changes in the TRPV1 pore are currently under intensive investigation and are thought to involve movements of S6 and the selectivity filter (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018; Jara-Oseguera et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018; Jara-Oseguera et al., 2019

claim: Capsaicin has a distribution of hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups that matches complementarily to the electrostatic distribution of the ligand-binding pocket.
source: Our results from structurally related ligands revealed how the molecular structure of capsaicin makes it a very potent agonist for TRPV1: not only does it have a distribution of hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups that matches complementarily to the electrostatic distribution of the ligand-binding pocket, but also the separation between the hydrogen bond-forming groups (an amide in the neck and a hydroxyl group in the head) matches perfectly the distance between T551 in S4 and E571 in the S4-S5 linker in the permissive conformation.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: The separation between the hydrogen bond-forming groups in capsaicin matches perfectly the distance between T551 in S4 and E571 in the S4-S5 linker in the permissive conformation.
source: Our results from structurally related ligands revealed how the molecular structure of capsaicin makes it a very potent agonist for TRPV1: not only does it have a distribution of hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups that matches complementarily to the electrostatic distribution of the ligand-binding pocket, but also the separation between the hydrogen bond-forming groups (an amide in the neck and a hydroxyl group in the head) matches perfectly the distance between T551 in S4 and E571 in the S4-S5 linker in the permissive conformation.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: The size mismatch of Cap-1 and Cap+1 likely causes these agonists to be not as stable as capsaicin in the vertical binding pose.
source: Cap-1 and Cap+1, being about 1.5 Å shorter or longer than capsaicin, respectively, can form these hydrogen bonds. However, the size mismatch likely causes these agonists to be not as stable as capsaicin in this binding pose.
evidence: Supported by inference from computational modeling and experimental data

claim: Cap-1 and Cap+1 explore other low-energy binding poses due to size mismatch in the vertical pose.
source: However, the size mismatch likely causes these agonists to be not as stable as capsaicin in this binding pose. Therefore, they explore other low-energy binding poses.
evidence: Supported by inference from computational modeling and experimental data

claim: The alternative binding poses for Cap-1 and Cap+1 are not as stable as the vertical pose of capsaicin.
source: The alternative binding poses are not as stable as the vertical pose of capsaicin, as the computational modeling results revealed (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and reference to Figure 3

claim: When T551 and E571 were simultaneously mutated to a hydrophobic residue, capsaicin became a less potent agonist but could still induce strong channel activation at high concentrations.
source: The existence of alternative binding poses for capsaicin analogs is not surprising; indeed, when the two hydrogen bond-forming residues, T551 and E571, were simultaneously mutated to a hydrophobic residue to prevent the vertical pose, capsaicin became a less potent agonist but nonetheless could still induce strong channel activation at high concentrations (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015

claim: Capsaicin can bind in an alternative pose(s) when the most favorable binding pose is prohibited.
source: This observation suggested that capsaicin must also be able to bind in an alternative pose(s) when the most favorable binding pose is prohibited.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: The electrostatic potential distribution inside the ligand-binding pocket might play an important role in ligand binding.
source: While it remains to be explored what other factors are present, we speculate that the electrostatic potential distribution inside the ligand-binding pocket might play an important role.
evidence: Speculative statement based on observations

claim: The binding poses of the two capsaicin analogs are stabilized by both polar and nonpolar interactions.
source: Our study revealed that the binding poses of the two capsaicin analogs are stabilized by both polar and nonpolar interactions.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: Progressively shortening capsaicin's hydrophobic tail led to incremental right-shifts of the concentration-response curve, with an associated increase in EC50 by as much as three orders of magnitude.
source: While VDW interactions are in general harder to pinpoint and prove in functional tests, we have previously shown that progressively shortening capsaicin's hydrophobic tail led to incremental right-shifts of the concentration-response curve, with an associated increase in EC50 by as much as three orders of magnitude (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015

claim: The horizontal pose of Cap+1 prevented the tail from going deep into the highly hydrophobic upper region of the ligand-binding pocket.
source: In the present study, we observed from Cap+1 that the horizontal pose prevented the tail from going deep into the highly hydrophobic upper region of the ligand-binding pocket.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: The resultant loss of VDW interactions likely contributes to the reduced potency of Cap+1.
source: The resultant loss of VDW interactions likely contributes to the reduced potency of this analog.
evidence: Supported by inference from computational modeling and experimental data

claim: F544 in the hydrophobic upper region contributes substantially to VDW interaction with the tail of capsaicin and Cap-1.
source: Indeed, F544 in the hydrophobic upper region is found to contribute substantially to VDW interaction with the tail of capsaicin (Yang et al., 2015) and Cap-1 (Figure 3B); a hydrophilic residue at the equivalent position of TRPV2 (S498) needed to be mutated to a phenylalanine in order to introduce capsaicin binding to the capsaicin-insensitive TRPV2 (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 3B

claim: A hydrophilic residue at the equivalent position of TRPV2 (S498) needed to be mutated to a phenylalanine in order to introduce capsaicin binding to the capsaicin-insensitive TRPV2.
source: Indeed, F544 in the hydrophobic upper region is found to contribute substantially to VDW interaction with the tail of capsaicin (Yang et al., 2015) and Cap-1 (Figure 3B); a hydrophilic residue at the equivalent position of TRPV2 (S498) needed to be mutated to a phenylalanine in order to introduce capsaicin binding to the capsaicin-insensitive TRPV2 (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016

claim: The ligand-binding pocket is mostly electro-neutral to accommodate a native lipid molecule in the closed conformation and capsaicin in the open conformation.
source: The ligand-binding pocket, on the other hand, is mostly electro-neutral to accommodate a native lipid molecule in the closed conformation (Gao et al., 2016; Figure 5—figure supplement 4, left) and capsaicin in the open conformation (Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013; Figure 5—figure supplement 4, right).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gao et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013 and references to supplementary figure

claim: Local changes in electrostatic potential distribution occur as the ligand-binding pocket moves from apo to permissive state.
source: While the overall polarized electrostatic potential distribution inside the ligand-binding pocket remains undisturbed, local changes clearly occur as the ligand-binding pocket moves from apo to permissive state.
evidence: Supported by inference from structural analysis

claim: The electrostatic potential distribution of capsaicin or its analog are distinct.
source: Because the electrostatic potential distribution of capsaicin or its analog are distinct (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), the electrostatic influence on them is likely to be different.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis and reference to supplementary figure

claim: There is a side portal in the ligand-binding pocket that is directly accessible to the electro-negative pore.
source: Of particular notice is the presence of a side portal in the ligand-binding pocket that is directly accessible to the electro-negative pore (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, right panel).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and reference to supplementary figure

claim: The side portal is not observed in the apo state and is associated with the conformational changes during activation.
source: As the presence of this portal, not observed in the apo state, is associated with the conformational changes during activation, ligands interacting distinctly with it are expected to exert an energy bias toward allosteric activation.
evidence: Supported by inference from structural analysis

claim: Introducing a single halogen atom (Cl, Br or I) to the head of either capsaicin or RTX could turn these TRPV1 agonists into competitive antagonists.
source: Indeed, introducing a single halogen atom (Cl, Br or I) to the head of either capsaicin or RTX could turn these TRPV1 agonists into competitive antagonists (Appendino et al., 2003; Wahl et al., 2001; Appendino et al., 2005; Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by citations to Appendino et al., 2003; Wahl et al., 2001; Appendino et al., 2005 and reference to supplementary figure

claim: In TRPV1, the ligand recognition mechanism has evolved following the allosteric principle.
source: Therefore, in TRPV1, the ligand recognition mechanism has evolved following the allosteric principle.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data and computational modeling

claim: A full agonist and a partial agonist are distinguished by their ability to stabilize the permissive conformation, governed by distinct ligand-receptor interactions inside the ligand-binding pocket.
source: A full agonist and a partial agonist are distinguished by their ability to stabilize the permissive conformation, governed by distinct ligand-receptor interactions inside the ligand-binding pocket (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 5D
